rotational-inertia-s2.title: Moving two sliders out on a platform
rotational-inertia-s2.text: Two 0.50 kg sliders sit on a light platform, one each side of its axis, each a distance r from the axis. A student measures the rotational inertia of the platform and sliders for four values of r.

items.q: What is the rotational inertia of the rod and balls about axis A? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that uses r instead of r². I = Σmr².
Value: that puts the middle ball 0.40 m from axis A. It sits on the axis, so its r is zero.

why.correct: The middle ball is on axis A (r = 0). I = 2(0.20 kg)(0.40 m)² + 0 = 0.064 kg·m².

items.q: What is the rotational inertia about axis B?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the inertia about axis A. About B, each ball’s distance is measured from the end.
Value: that uses r instead of r². I = Σmr².

why.correct: About B: the near ball has r = 0, the middle ball r = 0.40 m, the far ball r = 0.80 m. I = 0 + (0.40 kg)(0.40 m)² + (0.20 kg)(0.80 m)² = 0.064 + 0.128 = 0.192 kg·m², about 0.19 kg·m².

items.q: Why is the rotational inertia about axis B larger than about axis A, although the mass is the same?
options: The mass is, on average, farther from axis B
Axis B is at the end, where the rod is heavier
Axis B passes through less of the mass
Rotational inertia is larger about any axis at an end

why.correct: I = Σmr². About B the 0.20 kg ball is 0.80 m away, and r² makes that distant mass count four times as much as at 0.40 m. Same mass, spread farther from the axis: larger I.
options: Right: I depends on how far the mass is from the axis, as r².
The rod is light; its ends are not heavier. The distances to the axis change.
Axis B passes through a 0.20 kg ball; axis A through the 0.40 kg ball. What matters is how far the rest is.
An end axis gives a larger I here because of the distances, not because it is an end.

items.q: Axis A passes through the center of mass. Which expression gives the inertia about axis B from the inertia about axis A?

why.correct: Parallel-axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md², with M the total mass (0.80 kg) and d the distance between the axes (0.40 m): 0.064 + 0.128 = 0.192 kg·m², which matches the direct sum.
options: Right: parallel-axis theorem, total mass 0.80 kg moved 0.40 m.
The theorem uses the total mass of the system, 0.80 kg.
d is the distance between the two parallel axes, 0.40 m.
Moving the axis away from the center of mass increases I.

items.q: The two end balls are slid in to 0.20 m from the middle. The rotational inertia about axis A becomes
options: one quarter as large
half as large
the same
twice as large

why.correct: Only the end balls contribute about A, each as mr². Halving r multiplies r² by ¼, so I goes from 0.064 to 0.016 kg·m².
options: Right: r halves, so each r² term is ¼ as large.
I depends on r², not r.
The mass is the same, but it is closer to the axis.
Moving mass toward the axis decreases I.

items.q: From the pattern in the data, what is the rotational inertia of the platform alone, with no sliders?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the first row, with the sliders 0.10 m out. Remove their 2mr² = 0.010 kg·m².

why.correct: Each row fits I = I_platform + 2(0.50 kg)r². At r = 0.10 m the sliders add 2(0.50)(0.10)² = 0.010 kg·m², so I_platform = 0.030 − 0.010 = 0.020 kg·m².

items.q: Which graph of these data is a straight line?
options: I against r²
I against r
I against 1/r
I² against r

why.correct: Two point sliders add 2mr², so I = I_platform + (2m)r². Plotting I against r² gives a straight line with slope 2m and intercept I_platform.
options: Right: I = I_platform + (2m)r² is linear in r².
I grows faster than r; the points curve upward.
I increases with r, so it decreases against 1/r along a curve.
Squaring I gives no linear pattern here.

items.q: What is the slope of the graph of I against r²?

why.correct: Slope = ΔI/Δ(r²) = (0.180 − 0.030) kg·m² / (0.16 − 0.01) m² = 1.0 kg, equal to 2m, the total mass of the two sliders.

items.q: Predict the rotational inertia with the sliders 0.60 m from the axis.
options: 0.38 kg·m²
0.32 kg·m²
0.36 kg·m²
0.27 kg·m²
This extends the last step as if I grew linearly with r.
This leaves out the platform’s own 0.020 kg·m².
This scales the 0.40 m value by 0.60/0.40, a linear guess.

items.q: The rotational inertia of an object about an axis depends on
options: its mass and how that mass is spread around the axis
its mass alone
how fast it is turning
the forces acting on it

why.correct: I = Σmr²: each bit of mass counts with the square of its distance from the axis, so both the mass and its distribution matter.
options: Right: I = Σmr².
Two objects of the same mass can have very different I.
I is a property of the mass and the axis, not of the motion.
Forces give torques; they do not change I.

items.q: A solid disk has mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.30 m. Its rotational inertia about its center is I = ½MR² (given). What is I?

mistakes.why: Value: R was not squared. I = ½MR².

why.correct: I = ½MR² = ½(2.0 kg)(0.30 m)² = 0.090 kg·m².

items.q: A thin hoop and a solid disk have the same mass and radius. Which is harder to start spinning about its center, and why?
options: The hoop, because all its mass is at the rim
The disk, because it is solid and has more material
Neither, because they have the same mass
The disk, because its mass is closer to the axis

why.correct: Rotational inertia measures resistance to changes in turning. The hoop’s mass sits at the rim (I = MR²); much of the disk’s mass is near the center (I = ½MR²), so the hoop is harder to spin up.
options: Right: the hoop’s mass is at r = R, so I = MR² > ½MR².
Same mass: the disk’s mass is spread inward, so its I is smaller.
Same mass, different distribution, different rotational inertia.
Mass close to the axis makes an object easier to spin, not harder.

items.q: A uniform rod has I = ¹⁄₁₂ML² about its center and I = ⅓ML² about one end (both given). The inertia about the end is how many times the inertia about the center?

why.correct: (⅓ML²)/(¹⁄₁₂ML²) = 12/3 = 4. About the end, much of the rod’s mass is far from the axis.
options: This compares the distances, not the inertias.
This reads only the denominator 3 and ignores the 1/12.
This reads only the denominator 12.

items.q: The same disk (2.0 kg, 0.30 m, I_cm = ½MR²) turns about an axis through a point on its rim, parallel to its central axis. What is its rotational inertia about that axis?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the inertia about the center. Add Md² for the shifted axis.
Value: that is only Md². Add the inertia about the center of mass.

why.correct: Parallel-axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md² = 0.090 + (2.0 kg)(0.30 m)² = 0.090 + 0.18 = 0.27 kg·m².

items.q: For a given object, about which of these parallel axes is the rotational inertia smallest?
options: The axis through its center of mass
An axis through its edge
An axis halfway between the center and the edge
It is the same about each parallel axis

why.correct: I = I_cm + Md², and Md² is zero only when the axis passes through the center of mass, so that axis gives the smallest I.
options: Right: I = I_cm + Md² is least when d = 0.
Moving the axis away from the center of mass adds Md².
This still adds Md² with d > 0.
The parallel-axis theorem shows I grows with d².

items.q: Two equal rings are threaded on a light rod that spins about its center. The rings slide outward, the same distance on each side. Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Rotational inertia of the system about the center
variables.why: The rings move farther from the axis, and each adds mr² with a larger r.

variables.name: Total mass of the system
variables.why: No mass is added or removed; it only moves.

variables.name: Position of the center of mass
variables.why: The rings move symmetrically, so the center of mass stays at the rod’s center.

why.correct: Moving the same mass farther from the axis raises I = Σmr², while the total mass and (by symmetry) the center of mass stay the same.
